titre: Halley and Clairaut: The Comet of 1759, Predicted and Then Corrected
accroche: In 1705, Halley announces the return of the comet of 1682. It is Clairaut who, in 1758, calculates the effect of Jupiter and Saturn, with a month's margin.
contenu_vulgarise:
The story is sometimes summed up in one sentence: Edmond Halley predicted the return of the comet of 1682, and it came back. That is true, and it is not enough. Halley died in 1742. The date the comet finally kept does not come from him.

## What Halley Saw

Halley studies comet orbits starting around 1695. He calculates that the comet of 1682 is the same as those of 1531 and 1607, whose returns are spaced 75 or 76 years apart, alternately. He concludes that the next appearance should not be expected before the end of 1758 or the beginning of 1759. A comet thus becomes a body that returns, and not an event that passes.

Halley also notes what complicates the prediction. The comet passed close to Jupiter in 1681, and the planet may have slowed its course. He notes that Jupiter's action on Saturn is enough to change the length of Saturn's period by a month. These discrepancies, he does not calculate.

## A Calculation by Three, Six Months of Work

In 1757, Joseph Lalande wants to establish a precise date for the return. It means calculating, step by step, what Jupiter and Saturn do to the comet. Alexis Clairaut supplies the basic plan, and Lalande asks Nicole-Reine Lepaute for help. Lalande will write that they calculated for six months, from morning to night, and that without her he could never have undertaken this enormous work.

On November 14, 1758, Clairaut announces to the Academy of Sciences that the comet will pass closest to the Sun, its perihelion, around mid-April 1759. He leaves a margin: so many small neglected quantities could easily make a month's difference. His calculation gives the period that is to end in 1759 about 618 days more than the previous one.

The comet is sighted as early as December 25, 1758. Charles Messier spots it in Paris on January 21, 1759. It passes its perihelion on the morning of March 13, a month before the announced date, at the edge of the margin Clairaut had declared.

## What the Episode Shows

The comet's return confirmed two distinct things. First, that comets return, which Halley had seen. Second, that Newton's gravitation makes it possible to calculate, planet by planet, what delays a body along its way: that is the work of Clairaut, Lalande, and Lepaute, which Halley had not been able to do.

In his 1760 *Théorie des comètes* (Theory of Comets), Clairaut does not name Lepaute among those who helped him with the calculations. He and Lalande will never again work together on an astronomy project.

repere.texte: In November 1758, Clairaut announces a passage of the comet at its perihelion around mid-April 1759, with a margin of one month. The comet reaches it on the morning of March 13, 1759.
repere.source: Messier, “A memoir, containing the history of the return of the famous comet of 1682,” trans. M. Maty, Philosophical Transactions, 1765

carte.punch: Halley saw that the comet would return. Clairaut calculated when, with a month's margin.
carte.idee: In 1705, Halley announces a return around late 1758. In November 1758, Clairaut calculates the effect of Jupiter and Saturn and predicts perihelion around mid-April 1759, with a margin of one month. The comet passes it on March 13, a month earlier.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: MacTutor — Nicole-Reine Etable de Labrière Lepaute
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; the biography of the computer without whom, Lalande said, he could not have done the work.

quiz.question: Why did Clairaut have to calculate the action of Jupiter and Saturn to predict the comet's return?
choix: Because Halley had been wrong about the identity of the comet of 1682
Because the comet had changed shape since its 1682 passage
Because Newton's law did not apply to comets without this correction
Because these planets alter the comet's path and lengthen its period
quiz.explication: The attractions of Jupiter and Saturn delay the comet: Clairaut counts about 618 more days for the period ending in 1759. Halley had identified the comet correctly, the comet's shape is not at issue, and Newton's law did apply, but using it required this calculation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Clairaut say about the margin of uncertainty in his prediction of perihelion?
choix: That it could be as much as a month, because of small neglected quantities
That it was zero, the calculation being complete
That it reached several years, for lack of data on Saturn
That it concerned only the date of the first sighting
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Clairaut announces mid-April 1759, specifying that the small quantities neglected by the approximations could make a month's difference. The comet passed on March 13, at the edge of this margin.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Halley rely on to assert that the comet of 1682 will return?
choix: Repeated observations of the comet throughout 1700
A complete calculation of the attractions of Jupiter and Saturn
The pairing of the comets of 1531, 1607, and 1682, with returns spaced 75 or 76 years apart
The agreement of the astronomers of his day with this hypothesis
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Halley identifies three appearances as a single comet and notes alternating intervals of 75 and 76 years. He has no calculation of planetary perturbations, which remains to be done in 1757-1758.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Lepaute's absence from Clairaut's Théorie des comètes in 1760 show?
choix: That Lepaute had not taken part in the calculations of 1757-1758
That a computer's role was left out, and that Lalande and Clairaut would no longer collaborate
That Lalande had written the entire Théorie des comètes alone
That Clairaut had redone all of Lalande's calculations alone
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lalande credits Lepaute with indispensable help during the six months of calculations. Clairaut does not name her in his 1760 work, which causes a falling-out and ends Lalande's collaboration with him.
